📚 Today you learned

Negative Free Cash Flow During a Capex Supercycle

A company turning FCF-negative usually screams distress. Not always — context matters. GOOG just went cash-flow negative in Q2 for the first time, and long-term debt jumped 111% to $98B, because capex is running at ~$175B this year building AI data centers. That's not a company that can't pay its bills; it's a company borrowing cheaply to build capacity for demand it believes is coming (see Day 11/29's hyperscaler-capex math — this is that spend, from the other side of the balance sheet). The tell that separates this from real distress: is the capex discretionary/growth or forced/maintenance? Growth capex you can slow down if the thesis breaks. The risk isn't insolvency, it's a demand miscalculation — if hyperscaler AI revenue doesn't show up on the timeline being bet on, that debt was for capacity nobody needed. Your GOOG position isn't sized to that binary outcome, but it's the real second-order risk behind the position, bigger than the antitrust noise.

Also today: Behavioral vs. structural antitrust remedies — a court ordering a company to change conduct (licensing terms, data-sharing) is behavioral; forcing a breakup/divestiture is structural. GOOG dodged a structural remedy on its ad exchange this week — the more common and less damaging outcome in modern US antitrust enforcement.
